title: Metadata replication caused global API failures
Root cause: Software bug: a new feature in the Service Control binary lacked appropriate error handling (null pointer check) and was not protected by a feature flag, allowing an untested code path to execute.
Amplifier: As the quota management tool tasks restarted, they created a thundering herd effect that overwhelmed the database. No backoff made the situation worse.
Trigger: Blank fields in some of the metadata for the quota management tool caused null pointer crashes
Fixing approach: SREs deployed a "red-button" configuration to disable the failing policy serving path and manually throttled task creation in large regions to prevent infrastructure collapse.
Mitigation approach: he architecture will be modularized to "fail open," global data replication will move to an incremental/canary model, and all critical changes will be enforced via feature flags and randomized exponential backoff.ion requests and direct to multi-regional infrastructure

title: Monolithic database lockup
Root cause: Architectural coupling of the build queue to the primary application database, which created a single point of failure and contention under high write volume. Additionally, the system lacked sufficient isolation between queue management and core data persistence.
Amplifier: A vicious positive feedback loop where database latency caused build timeouts, which in turn triggered automatic re-enqueuing of builds, exponentially increasing the write load on the already failing database.
Trigger: Thundering herd / Surge in GitHub pull / build requests, much more than usual
Fixing approach: First, they tried sizing down load balancer (bad!). Then they deployed new DB to new hardware and duplicated everything
Mitigation approach: The engineering team accelerated the decoupling of the build scheduling infrastructure to move the queue off the main DB and implemented better query optimization. They also established permanent hardware upgrades to provide more operational headroom.

title: Retry storm to an outdated backend makes service exceed regional capacity
Root cause: A software bug due to which the API would keep requesting stuff to an old backend even if a new one was available
Amplifier: Retry storm of APIs that kept overloading the old backend with requests until they exceeded its regional capacity
Trigger: The rollout of a new backend
Fixing approach: Delete credentials that were known to be failing, to stop the retry storm
Mitigation approach: Patch the software bug

title: Legacy client overwhelmed an underprovisioned service
Root cause: Popcount (internal service) was underprovisioned
Amplifier: Legacy desktop clients lacked backoff, and kept retrying to make requests to Popcount, overwhelming it
Trigger: Dependency introduced in new feature rolled out spawned too many requests for Popcount
Fixing approach: Quick fix in Popcount, didn’t work because of legacy clients. Had to firewall all clients out, since only that triggered their built-in backoff retryer
Mitigation approach: Fixed the client-side retry logic, implemented TTL caching for Discovery data, and decoupled/rate-limited non-critical log streams to prevent I/O saturation.

title: EBS Re-mirroring storm
Root cause: EBS does not handle correctly the case in which the volumes are isolated
Amplifier: Re-mirroring storm: all EBS volume try to replicate at the same time. This knocks out the control plane as well. The whole region is out!
Trigger: Incorrect traffic shift moved traffic to lower capacity network instead of secondary network
Fixing approach: Disable “Create volume” EBS APIs; Disable connection between degraded EBS volumes and the normal ones
Mitigation approach: Carry additional safety capacity (= add more EBS infrastructure) needed for large scale failures. Modify the retry logic to prevent re-mirroring storms.

title: Over-reservation of resources
Root cause: Misconfiguration in circuit breaker. Misconfiguration in rate limiters. Services reserved way more resources than they needed.
Amplifier: Retry storm; clients kept retrying and circuit breaker and rate limiters did not stop them.
Trigger: Run out of resources and could not handle the traffic spike
Fixing approach: Shutting down non-critical services to free up CPU and RAM
Mitigation approach: Fix retry circuit breakers and rate limiters. Make it harder for bots to storm the website.

title: DNS-Triggered EBS memory leak, storm
Root cause: Hidden memory leak
Amplifier: The system kept trying to failover even where there were not enough instances available.
Trigger: DNS update gone wrong makes EBS storage nodes completely filled up
Fixing approach: The team manually reduced the failover rate to stabilize the cluster and then identified and killed the misbehaving agents to free up system memory.
Mitigation approach: AWS committed to deploying a permanent fix for the memory leak, implementing per-process memory limits/monitoring, and improving the reliability of internal DNS propagation.

title: Cache invalidation is notoriously hard. If you mess it up at Meta, Facebook goes down!
Root cause: A faulty software that changes the cache
Amplifier: The fact that the values were incorrect made more and more clients request again stuff to the DB, which made it fail, which made more clients request stuff to the DB…
Trigger: A change to the persistent copy of a configuration value that was interpreted as invalid
Fixing approach: Shut down the whole service
Mitigation approach: Redesign architecture

title: Internal network congestion: monitoring blackout!
Root cause: Bug in internal client backoff behaviour. Internal network architecture made congestion easier.
Amplifier: Internal clients kept retrying and the configured backoff didn’t work as intended; internal monitoring tools were hindered for the same reason as well.
Trigger: An automated activity designed to scale capacity for a service hosted in the main AWS network
Fixing approach: Remove congestion by moving traffic on other network paths, disable traffic-heavy services
Mitigation approach: AWS disabled the problematic scaling automation, committed to a fix for the client back-off code bug, and deployed new network configurations to protect gateway devices from traffic surges.

title: Flushing the cache caused a big cascading failure
Root cause: Lack of circuit breakers and architectural dependency on expensive queries
Amplifier: A vicious cycle where high database load caused timeouts that prevented the cache from warming up, combined with aggressive client retries (even if they had backoff + jitter) that sustained the overload even after the trigger was paused.
Trigger: A 25% rollout of a Consul agent upgrade that caused Memcached nodes to deregister and be replaced by Mcrib with empty, un-warmed cache nodes.
Fixing approach: SREs applied a restrictive throttle to client boot requests to shed load and modified the application to query only missing GDM data from database replicas instead of all shards.
Mitigation approach: Slack moved the groups DM data to a channel-sharded table to eliminate scatter queries, updated Mcrib to handle node churn more safely, and audited the fleet for other latent scatter query risks.

title: Thundering herd of millions of Discord users
Root cause: A latent bug in the presence cluster's membership logic that failed to handle node departures, leading to a split-brain state. This was compounded by an underlying Google Cloud hypervisor issue causing CPU soft locks.
Amplifier: Discord's session buffering mechanism; it attempted to store messages in memory for 1/3rd of all users whose connections were stalled by the presence failure, leading to rapid OOM crashes. Reconnection attempts made recovery harder.
Trigger: Thundering herd of reconnections after a 20-second soft lock on the CPU of one of their cluster servers.
Fixing approach: Operators globally disabled message sending to shed load, patched the API to throttle reconnection rates.
Mitigation approach: Discord deployed the presence split-brain fix, implemented "fast-fail" mechanisms and connection limits between sessions and presence, and improved automated detection for CPU lockups. No retry policy mentioned.

title: Little power loss makes DynamoDB metadata service collapse
Root cause: Insufficient provisioning and inadequate monitoring of the metadata service’s processing capacity.
Amplifier: A classic thundering herd effect where failing requests led to aggressive retries from storage nodes, creating so much load that operators were initially unable to even issue administrative commands to scale the metadata service.
Trigger: A brief, transient network disruption that forced a large portion of storage servers to simultaneously request membership data from the metadata service.
Fixing approach: Drastic step: pause all requests and enable to clean backlog, to finally be able to add hardware capacity
Mitigation approach: Added jitter; Increased metadata service capacity, implemented stricter monitoring on membership sizes, reduced the frequency of storage node check-ins,  began segmenting the metadata service into smaller, isolated cells.

title: Requests storm of treecaches to zookeepers (ahah)
Root cause: A design flaw in the TreeCache library that sends an unbounded, full-tree refresh request batch upon every connection flakiness event without back-pressure or session awareness.
Amplifier: A death spiral where connection flakiness triggered massive batches of refresh requests, which further overloaded ZooKeeper, leading to more timeouts and client OOM (Out of Memory) errors.
Trigger: High CPU load and GC pauses on the ZooKeeper (Elastic’s coordination layer) leader, causing client heartbeats to time out.
Fixing approach: New Zookeeper leader election; scale out to handle higher load
Mitigation approach: Developed and deployed TreeWatcher, a custom replacement for TreeCache that supports session resumption, implements server-driven back-pressure, and cancels redundant refresh cycles.

title: MongoDB saturated, but to fix it you break everything
Root cause: Absence of client-side connection pooling limits, which allowed services to create an unbounded number of connections that eventually saturated the database's available resources.
Amplifier: Human error during the rollback process; a misconfiguration forced all traffic from the secondaries to the primary, turning a slow read issue into a total primary node failure.
Trigger: A gradual, unexplained increase in connections to MongoDB secondary nodes, coinciding with configuration changes deployed the previous day.
Fixing approach: Resized MongoDB instances to handle higher connection volume, applied server-level connection limits, and corrected routing configurations to restore secondary read preferences.
Mitigation approach: Implemented hard connection limits across all services, permanently increased cluster hardware specifications, and deployed redundant tracking infrastructure in a separate region. Nothing retry-related.

title: What comes up must first go down
Root cause: A latent implementation bug in the feature flag logic where hosts, once told to stop writing to the database, would never resume trying even after the flag was toggled back without a full reboot.
Amplifier: The "Main" RDS database acted as a single point of failure; as the cache failed, a "read storm" overloaded MySQL, increasing the probability of hitting a rare concurrency race condition/deadlock.
Trigger: Toggling a feature flag to move database writes between Retriever clusters, which accidentally permanently disabled the "last written" timestamp updates for the schema cache.
Fixing approach: Manual circuit breaking; hard failover to MySQL replica
Mitigation approach: Removed the faulty code that allowed writes to be disabled behind the cache, completed the infrastructure migration, and began architectural reviews to further decouple the ingestion path from the primary database.

title: Slow servers, retry storms, and manual cleanups
Root cause: A performance regression in a new software release of the networking control plane caused requests to be processed too slowly to maintain throughput, leading to an unbounded queue growth.
Amplifier: A classic "retry storm" where client systems increased load via automated retries, coupled with a lack of automation to clear "stuck" state transitions in the database.
Trigger: The deployment of a faulty networking control software update that contained the performance regression.
Fixing approach: Engineers allotted more resources to sharded components, implemented emergency rate limits to throttle incoming requests, and performed a hard restart of the distribution service to flush the backlog.
Mitigation approach: Continuous load testing in the deployment pipeline, rate limiting of requests to control plane, further sharding of the global distribution service, and the development of automated tools to "unstick" failed operations without manual intervention.

title: Big october DNS AWS outage
Root cause: A latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS Enactor architecture where a stale check allowed an older plan to overwrite a newer one, which was then deleted by a cleanup process, leaving the service with an empty DNS record.
Amplifier: Textbook cascading failure: EC2 DropletWorkflow Manager (DWFM) collapsed because recovery attempts timed out due to sheer volume, and NLB health check death spirals where healthy instances were marked unhealthy due to delayed network state propagation
Trigger: Unusually high processing delays for one specific DNS Enactor instance, which then led to the overwriting of one DNS field with an empty field.
Fixing approach: Manual restoration of the DynamoDB DNS state by operators, followed by selective restarts of DWFM hosts and the temporary disabling of automatic NLB health check failovers to stop the capacity-removal cycle.
Mitigation approach: Disabling global DNS Enactor/Planner automation until the race condition is patched, implementing "velocity controls" on NLB capacity removal, and enhancing EC2's data propagation throttling to be queue-size aware.

title: Cloudflare
Malformed URLs bring down crates download
Root cause: The codebase was structured in a way that made testing environment-specific URL paths difficult, resulting in a refactor that lacked test coverage for production-variable logic.
Amplifier: The Cargo package manager's automated retry logic multiplied the request volume, which initially obscured the error as a potential traffic spike rather than a code bug.
Trigger: The promotion of the faulty staging deployment (with a typo in the URL) to the production environment
Fixing approach: Manual rollback
Mitigation approach: he team implemented tests using realistic production-style environment values and updated the staging smoke-test checklist to explicitly include crate downloads. Long-term plans include automating these smoke tests and establishing formal rules for when code reviews are mandatory.

title: What if the outage outages the management tools to fix the outage?
Root cause: A software bug in maintenance automation allowed it to deschedule multiple independent software clusters concurrently, combined with a misconfiguration that marked critical network control plane jobs as stoppable during maintenance.
Amplifier: A circular dependency where network congestion broke the management tools required to fix the network, and the loss of the control plane caused configuration data to be wiped, necessitating a slow, manual rebuild of the environment.
Trigger: The initiation of a "normally-benign," relatively rare maintenance event in a single physical location.
Fixing approach: Halting the faulty automation software, manually re-enabling the network control plane, and rebuilding/redistributing lost configuration data across multiple locations.
Mitigation approach: Hardening cluster management software to reject multi-location descheduling, reconfiguring control plane jobs to persist data locally, and ensuring the network can "fail static" for much longer periods without dropping routes. Not really anything retry-related.

title: Throttling is good, but if it’s generically global and strict…
Root cause: Global API request limit (API throttling) that was too strict; it lacked sufficient isolation between internal service traffic and external customer traffic.
Amplifier: The global nature of the quota meant that a localized spike from an internal service was "promoted" to a worldwide outage, leaving no region unaffected.
Trigger: An internal Google management service malfunctioned, generating a massive surge of requests that exceeded the Filestore API's global threshold.
Fixing approach: Engineers manually identified the rogue internal service and paused its operation to immediately relieve the pressure on the API.
Mitigation approach: Removing that specific global quota and place local limits instead. More granular monitoring.

title: GitHub
Root cause: A configuration mismatch where the automated failover tool was permitted to promote a remote database to "primary" status, despite the application layer being unable to handle the resulting cross-country latency.
Amplifier: The "split-brain" state: writes existed on the East Coast that weren't on the West, and vice versa. This prevented a simple automated "fail-back," forcing a slow manual rebuild from remote cloud backups.
Trigger: Routine maintenance to replace networking optical equipment that caused a 43-second network loss between the US East Coast network hub and the primary data center.
Fixing approach: Blocking everything (circuit-breaker-like), pausing high-volume write background jobs (Webhooks and Pages), restoring multiple terabytes of MySQL data from backups, and slowly syncing replicas until they could handle production load.
Mitigation approach: Reconfiguring the automated failover tool to prevent cross-regional primary promotions, accelerating "active-active" multi-datacenter architecture, and implementing chaos engineering to test failure scenarios.

title: If you don’t have monitoring, you don’t realize when you have problems…
Root cause: A Single Point of Failure in the task processing architecture and a latent bug/misconfiguration that caused the task retrieving daemon to lose its current state and default to an old timestamp upon restart.
Amplifier: A total lack of automated monitoring delayed detection for 4.5 hours, and the system’s "first-in, first-out" processing of the massive historical backlog created a vicious cycle of increasing latency.
Trigger: Human error resulting in the accidental restart of the wrong blade server
Fixing approach: Engineers manually reset the task counter to the current date, increased processing efficiency limits, and deleted millions of stale or non-essential tasks to clear the queue
Mitigation approach: Add monitoring logic!

title: Internal files should be reviewed with the same scrutiny as external ones, otherwise…
Root cause: Internal software had a limit on the size of a certain file, which when surpassed would cause the control plane to crash.
Amplifier: Cascading effect on other services. Requests backlog and retries sent down other parts of the infrastructure. Automated observability and debugging systems consumed massive CPU cycles to "enhance" the error reports from the panics, which increased latency and effectively self-inflicted a resource exhaustion state across the network.
Trigger: Change to one of their database permission system that caused the file to double in size.
Fixing approach: Engineers stopped the propagation of the bad feature file, manually rolled back to a known-good version in the distribution queue, and scaled the infrastructure up.
Mitigation approach: Hardening configuration ingestion to treat internal files with the same scrutiny as user input, implementing global "kill switches" for specific modules, and decoupling error-reporting resource consumption from core traffic processing.
